content: Good evening. I have to say, this has been one of the most exhausting and exhilarating weeks of my life. We opened on November 4 and I honestly haven't slept more than five hours any night since. But I'm here, I'm still standing, and I have numbers to share. Are you ready to hear how the first three days went?

Ready and genuinely curious. Opening week data is some of the most valuable — and most easily misread — information a new restaurant generates. There's so much noise from the novelty factor, from staff still finding their rhythm, from a customer mix that hasn't settled into your real core demographic yet. But it's also when your original projections meet reality for the first time, and that collision is always instructive. Walk me through it. What's the headline?

The headline is: dinner was strong, lunch is behind, and I'm trying to figure out whether the lunch situation is a real problem or just early-days noise. Let me give you the full picture. The November 4 grand opening went smoothly, fully booked — I mean that literally, every seat in the room. We had 28 covers for dinner that first night and service ran almost perfectly considering it was day one. The team was nervous but we held it together. I didn't sleep at all that night. Just sat at the bar after everyone left and went through the checks and tried to convince myself it was real.

A fully booked opening night where service held together is not something you should take for granted — kitchens and front of house teams routinely fall apart on day one because the rehearsals never fully simulate the real pressure. The fact that it ran 'almost perfectly' on that specific night is meaningful. But you said dinner was strong across the first three days, plural. Give me the actual numbers — covers each night — and your targets, because that's where we can start to get precise about what 'strong' really means.

Right, so here are the dinner covers for the first three days: 22, 26, 24. Against a target of 28 per night. So we were below target every night, but the opening night number — the 22 — actually felt misleading because we had two no-shows from the reservation list and one table that arrived 45 minutes late and disrupted the second seating flow. If I back those out mentally, night one was actually quite solid. Nights two and three, the 26 and the 24, felt more like steady-state operation at this stage. We weren't scrambling but we weren't packed.

Let me put some structure around that. Your dinner covers first three days: 22, 26, 24 against target 28. That's an average of 24 against a target of 28 — you're running about 86 percent of target over three nights, which is genuinely not bad for a brand-new restaurant in opening week. The no-shows and the late table on night one are real operational variables, not excuses. No-show rates of 7 to 10 percent are common in Tokyo Italian dining even for well-regarded restaurants, and you haven't yet built the relationship equity that makes guests feel accountable to your reservation. That will change. But I want to hear the ticket averages before I say more, because covers alone only tell half the story at a dinner-focused osteria in your positioning.

The ticket averages are actually the good news. Our actual dinner average ticket came in at 8,100 yen. We had projected something closer to 7,800 yen. So we're above projection on that metric even while we're below on covers. Guests are ordering more — more wine pairings than I expected, more of the composed antipasti plates, and the pasta-plus-secondi sequence is being ordered by probably 70 percent of dinner tables rather than the 50 percent I anticipated. People are settling in and eating properly, which is exactly what I wanted for the Osteria Morishita experience.

That's a genuinely meaningful signal and it deserves some unpacking. An actual dinner average ticket of 8,100 yen against a 7,800 yen projection — that's a 3.8 percent overage on average spend, which partially compensates for being below on covers. Let's do rough math: on a night with 24 covers at 8,100 yen average, you're generating about 194,400 yen in revenue. If you'd hit target covers of 28 at your original projected 7,800 yen average, that's 218,400 yen. So you're approximately 90 percent of your projected revenue even when covers are 86 percent of target, because the higher ticket is doing real work. More importantly, the behavior you're describing — the full pasta-plus-secondi sequences, the wine pairings, guests settling in — tells you that the people who are finding Osteria Morishita are your people. The room conversion is strong. Your issue right now is feeding the top of the funnel, not converting once they arrive. Now tell me about lunch, because you flagged it as the concern.

Lunch is where I'm less comfortable. We started November 5 lunch service — so that's only two days of data — and the covers have been 14, 18 against a target of 30. That's a pretty big gap. The first lunch felt almost empty to me. I know 14 covers in a 40-seat room is not a disaster but it didn't feel right. The second day improved, 18 is better, and there was a 4-person business lunch table that showed up without a reservation and we were able to seat them, which suggests some walk-in potential. But I'm looking at 30 as my target and I'm nowhere near it.

I want to be direct with you about this before we go further into interpretation, because the tendency when you're excited about a strong dinner opening is to categorize lunch as 'just getting started' without being honest about what the numbers actually imply. Lunch covers: 14, 18 against target 30. That's 47 and 60 percent of target respectively, and even the better day is significantly below where you need to be. This is a genuine performance gap, not just early noise. The question is whether it's a structural gap — meaning the Higashi-Azabu lunch market is thinner than you modeled — or an awareness gap, meaning the right customers don't know yet that you're open for lunch. Those require different responses. What's your intuition about which it is? And have you been outside the restaurant at lunch hour to actually observe the street traffic and who's moving through that stretch of 3-chome?

My intuition is that it's mostly awareness, but I'll be honest — I haven't stress-tested that belief yet. I've been so focused on dinner prep and managing the team that I haven't done the street observation you're describing. What I do know is that the lunch ticket is much lower than dinner. The actual lunch average ticket came in at 1,950 yen, which is more or less where I projected it. So it's not that guests are spending less than expected — it's purely a covers problem. The guests who come at lunch are doing what I expected them to do, ordering the pasta set and a drink. The room just isn't full enough.

The fact that your actual lunch average ticket of 1,950 yen is on track is actually important information — it tells you the lunch offer itself is landing correctly with the guests who find you. People aren't arriving and leaving disappointed or confused about what the menu is. They're ordering the pasta set, the ticket is where you expected, the experience is presumably working. This strongly supports the awareness hypothesis over the structural one. A structural lunch problem — wrong neighborhood, wrong price point, wrong format — would typically show up in weird ticket behavior, in early exits, in guests not returning. What you have instead is a thin but apparently satisfied cohort. The mission is now clearly defined: get more of the right people in the door between noon and 2pm. Before I give you specific recommendations, though, I want to ask about something else. Have you started getting any public reviews yet?

Yes — three Tabelog reviews came in and the first rating landed at 3.42. I have very mixed feelings about this. On one hand, I know 3.42 is not a bad Tabelog score for a brand-new restaurant with only three reviews. On the other hand, when I opened this place I was picturing something closer to 3.7 or 3.8 eventually, and seeing 3.42 as the starting number made my stomach drop a little when I first saw it. I keep reminding myself it's only three reviews. But I also know that early Tabelog scores carry a certain psychological weight and people do filter on them.

Your instinct to contextualize is correct, and I want to give you the honest picture. A 3.42 Tabelog rating after 3 reviews is a statistically meaningless data point in the strictest sense — three reviews is not a sample, it's three opinions — and in Tabelog's scoring algorithm, the weight of any individual early review is disproportionately high compared to what it will be once you have 30 or 50 reviews. The number will move, and it will move significantly based on who writes the next five to ten reviews. That said, your concern about the psychological weight is legitimate. Tabelog users who filter at 3.5 and above will not see Osteria Morishita in their search results right now, and in Tokyo that's a real narrowing of your discovery funnel during exactly the weeks when you most need new guests to find you organically. The practical question is: of the guests who have dined with you this week and had strong experiences — and based on what you've described, that sounds like the majority of your 70-something dinner covers across three nights — how many of them have you actively encouraged to leave a review? Not in a pushy way, but in a warm, personal way?

Honestly? Very few. I've been so focused on running service that the post-experience follow-up piece has been essentially nonexistent. I did personally speak with probably a dozen tables across the three dinner nights, and the feedback was overwhelmingly warm — people asking when we'd be open again, asking about the wine list, a few people asking about private dining for small groups. One woman told me it was the best tortellini in brodo she'd had outside of Italy, which I almost cried about. But I didn't translate any of that warmth into review requests. I think I need to fix that. The other thing I want to ask you about is whether there are any operational adjustments I should be thinking about right now, based on where the numbers are, or whether it's genuinely too early to make changes.

On review cultivation: yes, fix it, but do it in a way that fits the Osteria Morishita character. You're not running a volume operation where you hand every guest a card at checkout. What you're building is something more personal, and the review ask should match that. For guests who linger, who clearly had a meaningful experience — and you know who they are because you talked to them — a genuine, unhurried personal mention at the end of the evening is appropriate. Something like: we're just getting started and early voices on Tabelog matter a lot to us. Nothing transactional. The woman who said it was the best tortellini in brodo she'd had outside Italy? She should absolutely be writing a review. You may have left five or six of those on the table this week. On operational adjustments: here is my honest read. For dinner, I would not change anything structural right now. You are 86 percent of target on covers with tickets running above projection, and the guest behavior in the room is exactly what you designed for. The machine is working. Tinker with the wrong thing this early and you risk disrupting something that is quietly calibrating. For lunch, the situation is different — I do think there are specific moves worth considering now rather than waiting. The awareness gap has a two-week window where targeted action can bend the trajectory before habits form around your neighborhood. I'd suggest three things: first, identify the five or six office buildings and design firms within a ten-minute walk and personally introduce yourself to their front desks or office managers this week with a simple lunch menu in hand. Higashi-Azabu has real professional density that doesn't always express itself in foot traffic because those workers have existing routines. Second, consider whether your lunch Instagram cadence is showing the daytime offer clearly — not just the beautiful dinner plates but the pasta set at 1,950 yen, the natural light in your room at noon, something that signals 'we are here and open and worth your lunch break.' Third, the four-person walk-in group on your second lunch day is a lead worth following. If you can find out who they were — whether they're from a nearby firm, how they heard about you — that one table might be a thread that, pulled correctly, brings you a regular weekday cohort. First week data is fragile and I don't want to overfit to three days, but the directional message from your numbers is clear: protect and amplify what's working at dinner, run a targeted awareness campaign for lunch before the first two weeks are up. You have momentum. Don't let the lunch gap become a habit.

That's exactly the frame I needed. I think I've been looking at the lunch numbers with too much anxiety and the dinner numbers with too much relief, and neither reaction was quite right. The 22, 26, 24 dinner trajectory with an 8,100 yen average ticket — when I put it that way, that's actually a solid opening week for a 40-seat room in a neighborhood that doesn't have heavy foot traffic. And the lunch situation at 14 and 18 is real but it's fixable if I treat it like the awareness problem it probably is rather than a product problem. What I'm going to do this weekend is walk the neighborhood at lunch hour on Saturday and Sunday — not to work, just to observe. See where people are actually eating, what the street movement looks like, whether there are natural clusters I'm not accessing yet. And Monday I'm going to start the outreach you described. The 3.42 Tabelog rating I'm going to hold lightly until I have at least fifteen reviews. Does that sound like the right posture?

That sounds like exactly the right posture, and I want to say clearly: the fact that you're able to articulate it this precisely after only three days of operation, while sleep-deprived and in the middle of everything, is a good sign about how you're going to run this restaurant through harder moments than these. Your read is correct on all three fronts. The dinner numbers — 22, 26, 24 against target 28 with an actual average ticket of 8,100 yen — reflect a restaurant that is working at a fundamental level. The trajectory of night one to night two is directionally right, and the ticket overage tells you the experience itself is converting. The lunch numbers are a legitimate gap but an addressable one, and your instinct to observe before acting is methodologically sound — go see the neighborhood with your own eyes before you commit to any single theory about what the fix is. And holding the 3.42 Tabelog rating lightly until you have fifteen or more reviews is not wishful thinking, it's statistically appropriate. One more thing I'd add for this weekend: when you're walking the neighborhood at lunch on Saturday, pay specific attention to who is alone. Solo diners at lunch are an underserved segment in Italian restaurants at your price point, and if your counter seats or bar position allow for it, making solo guests feel genuinely welcome — not just tolerated — can become a distinctive feature that drives word-of-mouth in exactly the professional community you're trying to reach. Come back next week with the observational data and the outreach results. This is just the beginning of the picture.
